papers.title_in_file: Optimised Quantum Embedding: A Universal Minor-Embedding Framework for Large Complete Bipartite Graph
papers.what_it_is: A short arXiv preprint (2504.21112v1) that gives a periodic, closed-form minor-embedding procedure for complete bipartite graphs (RBM-shaped) on the D-Wave Pegasus topology and compares its embedding time and count of long chains against Minorminer for K(n,n) with n from 60 to 120; no annealer run is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the paper introduces an optimized minor embedding framework designed for mapping large complete bipartite graphs (e.g. Restricted Boltzmann Machines) onto adiabatic quantum processors, and describe it as a universal framework tailored to quantum annealers, notably leveraging the Pegasus topology.
quotes: This paper introduces an optimized minor embedding framework designed for mapping large complete bipartite graphs (e.g., Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs)) onto adiabatic quantum processors.
A universal minor-embedding framework tailored for efficiently embedding large complete bipartite graphs onto quantum annealers, notably leveraging the Pegasus topology.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope and target in Section I.
assertions.reader_inference: The word universal in the title is not tied to a stated class of graphs or hardware beyond complete bipartite graphs on Pegasus-like grids; only Pegasus is evaluated.

assertions.value: The authors benchmark their embedding framework against Minorminer for the Pegasus topology, and name extending the framework to alternative quantum hardware topologies, hybrid optimization techniques for qubit allocation and integration into real-world quantum-enhanced machine learning workflows as future work.
quotes: We benchmark our embedding framework against Minorminer, the default heuristic embedding algorithm, for the Pegasus topology
Future work will explore extending our embedding framework to alternative quantum hardware topologies
rating hybrid optimization techniques to refine qubit allocation further, and integrating these embeddings into real-world quantum-enhanced machine learning workflows.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own evaluation scope (Pegasus) and its future work in the Abstract and Section VI.
assertions.reader_inference: No other topology (Chimera, Zephyr) is tested, and no run on a physical annealer or on a machine learning workload is described anywhere in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors define minor embedding as mapping logical qubits onto interconnected physical qubit chains, ensuring logical connectivity by creating subtrees that effectively behave as single logical qubits, and state that the logical graph G is called a graph minor of the lattice U.
quotes: Minor embedding involves mapping logical qubits onto interconnected physical qubit chains, ensuring logical connectivity by creating subtrees that effectively behave as single logical qubits.
Each vertex of the logical graph G is mapped against a subtree and vertices of the graph U . G is called a graph minor of U [14].
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the definition its method depends on.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence in Section III-A is worded loosely: standard usage says the logical graph G is a minor of the hardware graph U, which is what the paper intends.

assertions.value: The authors state that when chains exceed a critical length threshold (typically more than six qubits long) they become increasingly prone to breakage due to thermal noise, fabrication imperfections and quantum decoherence, and that broken chains degrade the performance of the quantum algorithm.
quotes: When chains exceed a critical length threshold (typically more than six qubits long), they become increasingly prone to breakage due to thermal noise, fabrication imperfections, and quantum decoherence.
This leads to unreliable computational results, as broken chains disrupt the logical qubit representation and degrade the overall performance of the quantum algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unreferenced statement; the paper gives no citation or measurement for the threshold of six.
assertions.reader_inference: The threshold is used later as the metric cut-off, but no source for it is given in the text. Section V-A then says length six or above in one place and the table header says greater than 6 in another.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the Pegasus architecture each qubit has a nominal length of 12 and a degree of 15, and that the relation D = 12M (M − 1) gives the total number of qubits in Pegasus, where M is the number of vertical and horizontal cells.
quotes: In the Pegasus architecture, each qubit has a nominal length of 12 and a degree of 15.
The relation D = 12M (M − 1) gives the total qubits in Pegasus, where M is the number of vertical and horizontal cells.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the hardware with no citation attached at that sentence.
assertions.reader_inference: From the reader's background knowledge (not checked in this session; the coordinator should check Boothby et al., arXiv 2003.00133): the Pegasus graph P_M is usually given as 24M(M-1) qubits, not 12M(M-1). The paper's own Eq. 3 labels qubits over two orientations u, M values of w, alpha values of k and (M-1) values of z, a count of 2*alpha*M*(M-1), which with alpha = 12 is also 24M(M-1). So D = 12M (M − 1) looks inconsistent with the paper's own labelling.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference [15], that the largest clique embeddable on Pegasus is K12M−10, where M is the number of vertical and horizontal cells.
quotes: The theoretical maximum embedding of a complete graph (clique) is the largest clique embeddable is K12M−10 [15].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to another work, reference [15].
assertions.reader_inference: Not verified against [15] in this session.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing reference [15], that the theoretical maximum for a complete bipartite graph is max(Km,m) = K12M−20,12M−20, and give as the reason that bipartite graphs require fewer edges per node, thus allowing for larger embedding than complete cliques.
quotes: The theoretical maximum for complete bipartite graph (Km,n) is given by [15]:
This is because bipartite graphs require fewer edges per node, thus allowing for larger embedding than complete cliques.
assertions.certainty_reason: A bound the paper attributes to reference [15]; the paper does not derive it.
assertions.reader_inference: The reason given (fewer edges per node) is an informal argument, not a proof. Whether [15] states this bipartite bound could not be checked from this text.

assertions.value: The authors state that for P16 the maximum RBM theoretically embedded given by Eq. 1 is 172×172, and that embedding overhead (chains of qubits representing logical nodes) reduces the practical maximum size.
quotes: In practical application, embedding overhead (chain of qubits representation logical nodes) reduces the practical maximum size.
So for P16, the maximum RBM theoretically embedded given by Eq. 1 is 172×172.
assertions.certainty_reason: A figure obtained from the cited bound; the paper does not show the working beyond naming Eq. 1.
assertions.reader_inference: For M = 16, 12M − 20 equals 172, so the figure follows from Eq. 1. The paper later gives a different maximum for its own algorithm (K172,120), so 172 by 172 is a theoretical hardware bound, not what the algorithm reaches.

assertions.value: The authors state that the optimal embedding of complete bipartite graphs, ϵ : Ka,b → P, consists of a parallel path of horizontal qubits and a parallel path of vertical qubits.
quotes: The optimal embedding of complete bipartite graphs, ϵ : Ka,b → P , consists of a parallel path of horizontal qubits and a parallel path of vertical qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without a proof or a citation; the section is titled Theoretical Analysis but states no theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper states no optimality criterion (for example minimum total qubits or minimum maximum chain length) and gives no proof, so optimal is an assertion. The paper contains no theorem, lemma or proof.

assertions.value: The authors define a generic family of structured graphs G(M) with qubit count D = αM (M − 1), where α is a parameter defining the number of qubits directly connected to each qubit (the degree of the vertex), with qubits in vertical and horizontal orientations grouped into cells of fully connected vertices forming a complete bipartite graph Ka,b.
quotes: D = αM (M − 1)
where α is a parameter defining the number of qubits directly connected to each qubit (in other words, α is the degree of the vertex).
These qubits are grouped into cells of fully connected vertices (Kn), forming a complete bipartite graph Ka,b.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the generic topology its algorithm is written for.
assertions.reader_inference: Alpha is called the vertex degree here, but the requirement on the algorithm in Section III-B calls alpha the nominal length of the processor. For Pegasus the paper gives degree 15 and nominal length 12, so the two readings give different values.

assertions.value: The authors define a qubit (u, w, k, z) by orientation u (u = 0 vertical, u = 1 horizontal), perpendicular tile offset w, qubit offset k within a tile and parallel tile offset z, and define the integer labelling (u, w, k, z) → z + (M − 1)(k + α(w + M u)).
quotes: A qubit (u, w, k, z) in G is described by four parameters: u represents the orientation, where u = 0 for vertical and u = 1 for horizontal qubits.
The qubit offset k denotes the position of a qubit within a tile.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the coordinate system and labelling used by the algorithm.
assertions.reader_inference: The text is inconsistent on orientation: it says u = 0 is vertical, then calls the u = 0 qubit a left horizontal qubit, and maps visible nodes to horizontal qubits while computing their start index with u = 0. The argument order (u, z, k, w) used when the start indices are defined also differs from (u, w, k, z).

assertions.value: The authors state that each left horizontal qubit (u = 0) is connected to all vertical qubits within its own cell and to the bottom and top qubits in the adjacent cell to the right, that each right horizontal qubit (u = 1) is connected to all vertical qubits within its cell and the bottom and top vertical qubits in the neighbouring cell to the right, and that external connections (u, w, k, z) ∼ (u, w, k, z + 1) keep each qubit connected across the lattice.
quotes: Each left horizontal qubit (u = 0) is connected to all vertical qubits within its own cell, as well as to the bottom and top qubits in the adjacent cell to the right.
horizontal qubit (u = 1) is connected to all vertical qubits within its cell and the bottom and top vertical qubits in the neighbouring cell to the right
Additionally, the external connections (u, w, k, z) ∼ (u, w, k, z + 1) ensure that each qubit maintains connectivity across the lattice structure.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of hardware connectivity with no citation; it is also a simplified model of Pegasus.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a simplified connectivity model; it does not mention the odd couplers or the degree-15 structure of real Pegasus. The generic model's connectivity was not checked against the hardware graph.

assertions.value: The authors give, for V ≤ min(m, n)M, a number of vertical Km,n cells Hv = min(m, n) (a fraction with V as numerator, flattened by the text layer), and map each visible node k in a cell (w, k, z) to a physical horizontal qubit by V qubitid = startVid + α × k + z × (α × w) (Eq. 5) and each hidden node to a vertical qubit by Hqubitid = startHid + α × k + z × (α × (w + M )) (Eq. 6).
quotes: If V ≤ min(m, n)M , then the number of vertical Km,n cells we need is given by:
Hv = min(m, n)
V qubitid = startVid + α × k + z × (α × w) (5)
Hqubitid = startHid + α × k + z × (α × (w + M )) (6)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own mapping from logical nodes to physical qubit ids.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no proof that the mapping yields a valid minor (every visible-hidden pair adjacent through chains, chains connected, chains disjoint). Validity is shown only by example figures and by the run in Section V.

assertions.value: The authors state that when V > min(m, n)M, the first min(m, n)M visible (hidden) units use Eqs. 5 and 6 and the others use additional cells Hv,add = V mod min(m, n), with startVid given by Eq. 3 at (0, 0, 1, 1) and startHid by Eq. 3 at (1, 1, 0, 1).
quotes: If V > min(m, n)M , for the first min(m, n)M visible(hidden) units, we use the equations 5 and 6, and we embed the other visible (hidden node) using additional cells given by
Hv,add = V mod min(m, n)
startVid is given by Eq. 3 replacing (u, z, k, w) with (0, 0, 1, 1) and startHid is given by Eq. 3 replacing (u, z, k, w) with (1, 1, 0, 1).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own rule for the case where V exceeds the single-pass capacity.
assertions.reader_inference: No example or experiment in the paper uses this overflow case with a size stated for it, and the number of additional cells is given as a remainder rather than a ceiling quotient; this was not checked.

assertions.value: The authors state that the algorithm only requires that the nominal length of the processor satisfies alpha ≤ m + n + 1 to embed the structure in a physical architecture.
quotes: This algorithm only requires that the nominal length of the QAC processor is alpha ≤ m + n + 1 to embed this structure in a physical architecture
assertions.certainty_reason: A requirement stated without derivation.
assertions.reader_inference: With the paper's choice m = 4 and n = 8 the bound is 13, and the paper gives nominal length 12 for Pegasus. The paper does not derive the bound, and it uses alpha earlier as the vertex degree, which for Pegasus is 15.

assertions.value: The authors state that their embedding requires O(mn/d) physical qubits since the edges only exist between visible and hidden nodes and there is no intralayer coupling.
quotes: Our embedding requires O(mn/d) physical qubits since the edges only exist between visible and hidden, and no intralayer coupling reduces the number of virtual qubits per logical qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: An asymptotic claim stated without a derivation.
assertions.reader_inference: The symbol d is not defined in the text, and m and n are fixed hardware-cell constants, so the bound as written is not clearly an asymptotic statement in the graph size.

assertions.value: The authors state that the maximum RBM that can be embedded is given by max(Hidden) = (M − 1)n and max(Visible) = (3M − 2)m, each bounded by alpha M, and that the maximum complete bipartite graph that can be minor embedded on the Pegasus architecture using their algorithm is K172,120.
quotes: The maximum RBM (or complete bipartite graph) that can be embedded is therefore max(Hidden) = (M − 1)n max(H) ≤ αM and max(V isible) = (3M − 2)m with max(V isible) ≤ αM .
The maximum complete bipartite graph that can be minor embedded on the Pegasus architecture using this algorithm is K172,120.
assertions.certainty_reason: A capacity figure stated without a proof or a run at that size; the largest size run is 120×120.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints these formulas flat, so their exact form is uncertain. The paper does not show how 172 and 120 follow from them for M = 16, m = 4, n = 8, and the largest run reported is a 120×120 graph (Table I), so K172,120 was not demonstrated.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the Pegasus architecture with l = 12 they select m and n as 4 and 8, and that, for illustration, they embed an 8×16 RBM in which qubit 180 is mapped to visible node 0.
quotes: For the Pegasus architecture with l = 12, we select m and n as 4 and 8
For illustrative purposes, in this example, we embed an 8×16 RBM.
For example, qubit 180 is mapped to visible node 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the parameters of its own worked example.

assertions.value: The authors report for the worked example that visible node 0 connects to physical qubits 2970, 2985, 3000, 3015, 3030, 3045, 3060 and 3075, assigned to hidden nodes 0 through 7; that qubit 180 is coupled with qubit 181 to reach hidden nodes 8-15, mapped to physical qubits 3150 to 3255 in increments of 15; and that qubit 2970 is coupled with qubit 2971 and so on up to qubit 3075 with qubit 3076.
quotes: visible node 0 connects to a set of physical qubits with identifiers 2970, 2985, 3000, 3015, 3030, 3045, 3060, and 3075.
These qubits are logically assigned to hidden nodes 0 through 7
Qubit 180 is coupled with qubit 181, allowing visible node 0 to connect to an additional set of hidden nodes (8–15), which are mapped to physical qubits ranging from 3150 to 3255 in increments of 15.
qubit 2970 is coupled with qubit 2971, qubit 2985 with qubit 2986, and so on, continuing in this pattern until qubit 3075 is coupled with qubit 3076.
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked example given in prose and a figure; the paper does not state that the example was checked against the hardware graph.
assertions.reader_inference: The ids step by 15, which equals M − 1 for M = 16 in the paper's labelling, so the example is consistent with Eq. 3 for P16. The paper does not report the chain length or the total qubit count of this example.

assertions.value: The authors report that an 8×8 RBM requires a 2×2 grid of unit cells, that an 8×12 RBM requires two vertical columns and three horizontal rows, that a 44 × 44 RBM requires an 11 × 11 grid, and that a 60 × 60 RBM requires an 15 × 15 grid of Pegasus unit cells to ensure full connectivity between visible and hidden nodes.
quotes: In the case of an 8×8 RBM, the embedding requires a 2×2 grid of unit cells.
For an 8×12 RBM, the required structure expands to two vertical columns and three horizontal rows
As a result, the 44 × 44 RBM requires an 11 × 11 grid.
the 60 × 60 RBM requires an 15 × 15 grid of Pegasus unit cells to ensure full connectivity between visible and hidden nodes.
assertions.certainty_reason: Illustrative sizes given in prose with figures; the paper gives no derivation or check beyond the figures.
assertions.reader_inference: Each grid side equals the RBM side divided by 4, which matches m = 4. By the same rule a 120×120 RBM would need a 30 × 30 grid; the paper does not state that figure, and the 8×12 case (two columns by three rows) follows the same pattern of 4 units per cell.

assertions.value: The authors compare against Minorminer by embedding complete bipartite graphs Kn,n with n = 40 to n = 120 in increments of 20, using a fixed number of trials T equal to 100 for each configuration.
quotes: we have considered RBM to embed complete bipartite graphs Kn,n with n = 40 to n = 120 in increments of 20.
For a fixed number of trials T equal to 100 for each configuration, we define two metrics:
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the design of its own benchmark.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I in the text layer holds only 60×60, 80×80, 100×100 and 120×120; the n = 40 case named here has no row. Trials of a deterministic closed-form algorithm would give identical embeddings each time, so the 100 trials mainly vary timing; this is not said in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors define two metrics: the average time to embed (s), the average time required to produce the embedding, and the average number of chains with length ≥ 6, the chains longer than six; they state that a chain of length six or above is subject to breaking, so an embedding with a chain length of 6 or more produces unreliable results.
assertions.anchor: Section V-A, p.6; Table I header
quotes: average time to embed (s): This represents the average time required to produce the embedding
the average number of chains with length ≥ 6: this represent the chains longer than six.
embedding with a chain length of 6 or more produces unreliable results
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its own metrics in Section V-A.
assertions.reader_inference: The metric text says greater than or equal to 6 while the table header (Avg. Chains > 6) says greater than 6, and the text also says longer than six. The paper does not report chain length itself (mean, maximum or distribution), only the count of long chains. The claim that length 6 or more is unreliable is the unreferenced threshold of Section I.

assertions.value: The authors state that their embedding algorithm was run on a Dell R705X server with 128 logical cores and 503 GiB of RAM running Ubuntu 22.04 and Python 3.10.9, and that Minorminer 0.2.16 was used as the default D-Wave embedding algorithm for comparison.
quotes: Our embedding algorithm was used to run a Dell R705X server with 128 logical cores and 503 GiB of RAM.
The server ran Ubuntu 22.04 and Python 3.10.9.
Minorminer 0.2.16 was used to compare the results with the default D-Wave embedding algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper calls the setup hybrid but does not say where Minorminer ran, which Minorminer parameters (tries, timeouts, random seeds) or which target graph size were used, or whether the Minorminer timing includes graph construction. Without that, the timing comparison cannot be reproduced from the text.

assertions.value: The authors report in the abstract a 99.98% reduction in embedding time for a 120×120 complete bipartite graph, compared with Minorminer on the Pegasus topology.
quotes: Our empirical results show a 99.98% reduction in embedding time for a 120×120 complete bipartite graph.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with an undocumented baseline configuration.

assertions.value: The authors state that their method eliminates long qubit chains, which primarily cause decoherence and computational errors in quantum annealing, and that it significantly reduces the length of qubit chains compared with traditional minor-embedding approaches such as Minorminer, leading to enhanced robustness and reduced susceptibility to chain breakage.
quotes: Additionally, our method eliminates long qubit chains, which primarily cause decoherence and computational errors in quantum annealing.
We demonstrated that our embedding technique significantly reduces the length of qubit chains compared to traditional minor-embedding approaches such as Minorminer
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, supported by the long-chain counts in Table I only.
assertions.reader_inference: The only evidence is the count of chains at or above the threshold; chain length is not reported, nor are chain-break rates or solution quality on a physical annealer. Enhanced robustness is therefore inferred, not measured.

assertions.value: The authors state that their embedding algorithm allows for shorter qubit chains, reducing the risk of chain breakage and improving the accuracy of the annealing process, outperforms the heuristic Minorminer algorithm as shown in Table I, and efficiently identifies multiple RBM configurations in milliseconds.
quotes: Our embedding algorithm (Algorithm 1) allows for shorter qubit chains, reducing the risk of chain breakage and improving the accuracy of the annealing process
outperforms the heuristic Minorminer algorithm as shown in Table I.
our algorithm efficiently identifies multiple RBM configurations in milliseconds.
assertions.certainty_reason: The accuracy claim has no supporting measurement in the paper; the speed claim rests on Table I.
assertions.reader_inference: No annealing run, solution-quality or success-probability measurement is reported, so the accuracy of the annealing process was not tested. The per-embedding times of 0.012 s to 0.014 s read from the table fit the milliseconds statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that empirical evaluations demonstrate that their embedding approach enables faster embedding, at least two orders of magnitude faster than other metaheuristic approaches.
quotes: Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our embedding approach enables faster embedding (at least two orders of magnitude faster than other metaheuristic approaches)
assertions.certainty_reason: A general speed claim; only one baseline, Minorminer, is measured in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper compares only against Minorminer. The related work names template-based and Pegasus-specific methods [5], [7], [8] but none of them is benchmarked, so the plural other metaheuristic approaches is not covered by the evidence. The comparison is also between a closed-form constructive method and a randomized general-purpose heuristic.

assertions.value: The paper gives Algorithm 1, which takes as input n visible, n hidden, periodicity v, periodicity h and n periodicity and outputs logical-physical mappings for visible and hidden nodes and a coupling matrix J; its pseudocode sets J[a, b] to −1 for each (a, b) in the chain coupling list.
quotes: Algorithm 1 Embedding a Complete Bipartite Graph
Input: n visible, n hidden, periodicity v, periodicity h, n periodicity
Output: Logical-physical mappings for visible and hidden nodes, coupling matrix J
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its algorithm in Appendix A.
assertions.reader_inference: Algorithm 1 takes n visible and n hidden with a single periodicity, so it builds square K(n,n)-type graphs from periodic offsets; the general K(V,H) rule of Section III-B is not coded separately. The pseudocode is split across the page by the text layer but was read in full.

assertions.value: The authors state that setting Jij = 1 locks the two qubits together (antiferromagnetic coupling), which allows the formation of chains and extends connectivity beyond the rank-one (first-order) neighbourhood.
quotes: Setting Jij = 1 locks the two qubits together (antiferromagnetic coupling): this allows the formation of chains
extends the connectivity of physical qubits to qubits beyond the rank-one neighbourhood (first-order neighbourhood)
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the coupler convention with no citation, and it disagrees with the paper's own pseudocode.
assertions.reader_inference: Algorithm 1 sets chain couplings to −1, while this section says Jij = 1 locks qubits together. Locking two spins to the same value is a ferromagnetic coupling, which is a negative J in the common Ising convention, so antiferromagnetic here looks like a misnomer or a sign-convention difference. Not resolved by the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that early embedding techniques such as the TRIAD method often provide suboptimal embeddings for bipartite structures, that Serra et al. [5] demonstrated a template-based approach that significantly reduces embedding overhead, and that Goodrich et al. [7] alongside Zbinden et al. [8] presented systematic heuristics that achieve practical reductions in chain length for bipartite embeddings, particularly on Pegasus topologies.
quotes: Although these methods minimize coupler overhead for fully connected topologies, they often provide suboptimal embeddings for bipartite structures
Serra et al. [5] demonstrated a templatebased approach that significantly reduces embedding overhead
Goodrich et al. [7] alongside Zbinden et al. [8] presented systematic heuristics that achieve practical reductions in chain length for bipartite embeddings, particularly on Pegasus topologies.
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work; not verified here.
assertions.reader_inference: Neither the template-based method of [5] nor the Pegasus-specific heuristics of [7] and [8] are benchmarked in this paper, although the text names them as close prior work on the same problem. The reader could not verify references [7] and [8] from this text.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that quantum annealing approaches for RBM training have shown promise in generative modelling and anomaly detection, and that Quantum RBMs leverage the Ising Hamiltonian to implement the bipartite structure directly on quantum hardware, reducing simulation overhead and potentially enhancing performance.
quotes: Quantum Annealing approaches for RBM training have shown promise in generative modelling and anomaly detection
Quantum RBMs (QRBMs) leverage the Ising Hamiltonian to implement the bipartite structure directly on quantum hardware, reducing simulation overhead and potentially enhancing performance
assertions.certainty_reason: Statements the paper attributes to other work and states in hedged terms.
assertions.reader_inference: These are background claims about QRBM training, not results of this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that their findings advance the scalability of quantum embeddings, particularly for quantum generative models, anomaly detection and large-scale optimization tasks, and that by preserving the bipartite structure of RBMs their approach enhances the scalability of quantum machine learning models on quantum annealers.
quotes: These findings advance the scalability of quantum embeddings, particularly for quantum generative models, anomaly detection, and large-scale optimization tasks.
our approach enhances the scalability of quantum machine learning models on quantum annealers.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of relevance with no machine learning experiment behind it.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper runs no RBM training, generative-model or anomaly-detection workload; the only experiments are embedding time and long-chain counts. The scalability claim for QML is an extrapolation from the embedding result.

assertions.value: The authors state that their empirical results further confirm that their method enables the embedding of larger RBMs while maintaining computational efficiency, as indicated by the drastic reduction in embedding time and the elimination of long qubit chains.
quotes: Our empirical results further confirm that our method enables the embedding of larger RBMs while maintaining computational efficiency, as indicated by the drastic reduction
in embedding time and the elimination of long qubit chains.
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion that the reported measurements only partly support.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I reports Minorminer embeddings up to 120×120, the same largest size as the proposed algorithm, so the table does not show the proposed method embedding larger RBMs than Minorminer can; it shows faster embedding and fewer long chains at the same sizes. The sizes between 120 and the stated K172,120 maximum were not run.

assertions.value: The authors state that leveraging advances in error correction and improved qubit coherence times will further enhance the applicability of their embedding framework to large-scale practical problems.
quotes: leveraging advances in error correction and improved qubit coherence times will further enhance the applicability of our embedding framework to large-scale practical problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A forward-looking statement without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Stated as future work; the paper does not examine error correction or coherence.
